Hand-foot syndrome and palmo-plantar erythrodysesthesia

A 31-person double-blind split-body pilot reported better treated-side outcomes than sham and pain reduction in 49% of participants, with no adverse reactions reported. A later 40-person randomized study publication is a protocol and provides no completed results.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 31-person double-blind split-body pilot reported better treated-side outcomes than sham and pain reduction in 49% of participants, with no adverse reactions reported. A later 40-person randomized study publication is a protocol and provides no completed results.

Summary of the Evidence

Two unique titles map to hand-foot syndrome or palmo-plantar erythrodysesthesia. One is a completed 31-person split-body double-blind randomized pilot; the other is a 2024 publication describing a planned randomized trial, not completed clinical research. Counting the protocol as a trial result would overstate the evidence. No animal or laboratory study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

Latifyan and colleagues compared PBM with sham on opposite body sides in a small pilot. A blinded assessor found a statistically significant difference favoring the PBM-treated side, pain decreased in 49% of participants, and no adverse reactions were reported. The split-body design provides a direct sham comparison, but each participant contributes paired treatment areas and the study has not been independently replicated. Lestido and colleagues published a protocol for a planned randomized study of 40 people; it contains no outcome data and must not be counted as a completed efficacy trial (Latifyan et al. 2020 Lestido et al. 2024).

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone laboratory study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The completed pilot used red 660 nm LED treatment. The later protocol plans 630 nm LED at 4 J/cm² twice weekly for four weeks, with sham comparison; these are planned settings, not a tested regimen with published results. The protocols and evidence status should therefore remain distinct.

Interpretation

The small split-body trial supports a short-term signal for treated skin areas, while precision and replication remain limited. The protocol cannot yet add evidence about benefit or harms.

Evidence strength in source summaryShort-term pain and lesion outcomes versus sham: Low Evidence for a full parallel-group protocol: Not yet available
Publications and records2 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One small double-blind split-body randomized pilot reported a PBM-versus-sham difference and reduced pain, but it has not been independently replicated. A later publication is a randomized-trial protocol and reports no patient outcomes. Larger completed trials with symptom and lesion outcomes would improve confidence.
